question: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

According to Politico, the Commission is currently preparing a ‘gradual integration’ framework for candidate countries. This mechanism would allow selected economic benefits to be granted to candidate countries even before they formally accede. More specifically, this would include access to certain EU funding programmes, trade preferences and partial access to the single market. This may be particularly relevant in the case of Ukraine, whose accession process may take many years. Article 49 TEU sets out the Treaty procedure for accession to the Union, requiring the unanimous agreement of the Member States and ratification in accordance with their constitutional requirements. Granting candidate countries, especially Ukraine, benefits similar to membership outside this procedure could represent a significant departure from the current system and have serious legal, budgetary and economic implications. 1.

What specific legal basis in the Treaties does the Commission consider sufficient to grant candidate countries, especially Ukraine, partial access to the single market, EU programmes and EU funds before accession?
How will the Commission ensure that ‘gradual integration’ does not lead to a circumvention of Article 49 TEU or to a de facto predetermination of Member States’ decisions on Ukraine’s accession?
Will the Commission publish a legal assessment of the compatibility of this framework with the Treaties before presenting specific measures?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission considers Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to provide the legal basis for concluding association agreements with third countries, including candidate countries, establishing reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedures. In Ukraine’s case, the Association Agreement1, in force since 2017, already provides the basis for access to parts of the single market, subject to strict conditions, such as alignment with the EU acquis indicated in the Agreement. One example is Ukraine’s access to the EU-Roam-Like-at-Home area as of January 2026. In addition, there are several cases in which EU law already provides for the sectoral opening of the single market on the basis of specific third-country regimes, subject to the conditions laid down in the EU acquis. As regards EU funds and programmes, participation is based on bilateral agreements with the candidate countries. Under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU), accession remains a single, comprehensive process based on full acceptance of the rights and obligations of membership. Any pre-accession sectoral integration serves only to support convergence and preparation, in the EU’s interest; it neither replaces nor prejudges accession. The process remains fully governed by Article 49 TEU, with Member States in the Council deciding unanimously on each key step, including the opening of clusters, the closing of chapters and, ultimately, accession itself. Any specific gradual integration measure will be assessed in accordance with the applicable legal regime and considering the conditions set out therein. Where a measure requires a bilateral agreement, the legal basis will be set out in that agreement with the enlargement partner.
1 Consolidated text: Association Agreement between the European Union and the European Atomic Energy
Community and their Member States, of the one part, and Ukraine, of the other part; http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2014/295/2025-10-29.
